title: Patterns Take Data Apart
goal: match tests the shape of a value and binds its parts in one step.

sections.text: A `match` expression compares a value against patterns. A pattern does two jobs at once: it tests which shape the value has, and it binds the inner parts to names. For an enum variant like `Event::Click(x, y)`, one pattern checks the variant and gives you both fields.

sections.caption: One arm per shape. The compiler checks that no shape is missing.

sections.text: The compiler checks two things for you. First, exhaustiveness: a `match` must cover every variant, so adding a new variant later turns every incomplete `match` into a compile error. That is a feature. Second, shape: a pattern with the wrong number of fields is rejected with `E0023`.
The compiler cannot check meaning. `Event::Click(y, x)` compiles exactly like `Event::Click(x, y)` and swaps the coordinates. Field order in a pattern carries meaning that only tests can verify.

When only one shape is interesting, `if let Some(x) = value` is a smaller way to write a two-arm match. And the wildcard `_` matches anything, which also means it silently absorbs variants you add later. Prefer naming the variants you handle.

explanation: Patterns test shape and bind fields in one step. The compiler enforces exhaustiveness; the meaning of positions is on you.
